articles.title: Putin and Trump discuss Ukraine in 'extremely frank' call
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin and US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday discussed the Ukraine conflict in an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long...
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday discussed the Ukraine conflict in an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long phone call, the Kremlin said.

It came after US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend in an attempt to kickstart long-stalled US efforts to end the fighting.

Washington has been pushing for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv.

Kyiv says the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.

During their call on Tuesday, Putin and Trump "focused on the issue of a settlement in Ukraine", Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters including AFP.

Trump called for a speedy end to the fighting, Ushakov said, while Putin presented an "objective and detailed analysis" of the frontline situation.

Putin has routinely said his troops are advancing across the entire front, with the capture of the entire eastern Donbas region a matter of time.

Putin "pointed out what the Americans could realistically do to bring the hostilities to a swift conclusion" and stressed that Russia had "no aggressive plans" towards Europe, Ushakov added.

Trump and the White House did not provide an immediate readout of the call.

Russia has intensified aerial attacks on Ukrainian towns and cities in recent months.

After announcing a brief ceasefire to coincide with Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Kyiv, Moscow resumed strikes on the Ukrainian capital overnight, killing at least five people, according to Ukraine's rescue services.

AFP reporters in Kyiv heard fresh explosions in the early hours of Tuesday, triggering fires and sending locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter.

Zelensky meanwhile said Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this month for talks on finding an end to the war.

"If all sides agree, we also want to hold it in the autumn. If September works out, then it would be great. The earlier, the better," he said.

Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kyiv have shifted their positions.

"The moment the US president's peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said.

"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy."

Russia said it had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centres in Kyiv and its suburbs.

Locals told AFP how they ran for cover as the attack started.

"It was very terrifying, we barely managed to run into the parking lot. The parking lot was shaking all over too," Nina Kimova, 55, said, adding that her car had been "burnt to ashes".

Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia's offensive, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.

In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.

Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing for a de-escalation ahead of winter and that Putin did not want to annoy Trump before the US midterm legislative elections in early November.

Russia has struck Ukraine's energy grid each winter since launching its offensive in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20C.

The two sides appear no closer to agreeing on how the war should end.

Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support.

Kyiv has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

articles.title: A California woman built a 10,363-sq-ft French-style mansion with centuries-old materials sourced from around the world; no one has lived in it, and it is now asking $29M
articles.summary: News News: Maison de Campagne, a manor in Rancho Santa Fe, CA, is up for sale, according to a report by Realtor.com. The French-style home looks like it has a ba.
articles.body: Maison de Campagne, a manor in Rancho Santa Fe, CA, is up for sale, according to a report by Realtor.com. The French-style home looks like it has a backstory, with aristocrats and centuries-old family dinners, perhaps a scandal or two. But it doesn’t. This five-bedroom home does not have any complicated history; it was built with something old without being old. No one has lived in this 10,363-square-foot home, and now it is listed for $29 million.Bringing countryside charm to CaliforniaBarbara Lee Grigsby, the current owner and designer of the property, assembled a team of master artisans and sourced materials from across the world. She has one goal in mind: if you can’t buy history, you can at least buy the materials history leaves behind.She sourced antique roof tiles primarily from France. The wide oak flooring was milled from reclaimed stock. The limestone and marble were hand-picked. Even the ironwork and artisan lighting fixtures are custom-made. Grigsby also incorporated centuries-old architectural elements that she knew would be impossible to source again once construction wrapped. Every detail was curated to reflect her style.The most attractive factor about this listing is that the manor comes fully furnished, with antiques, gallery-acquired art and custom-made furniture.“For the discerning buyer, whose most valuable asset is time, Maison de Campagne offers something exceptionally rare: a complete and irreplaceable world, ready to be enjoyed from the moment of ownership,” listing agents Heather Manion and Ernie Carswell of Pacific Sotheby’s International Realty told the outlet.The best part? Nobody has lived in the manor yet.What does the buyer get?The manor is set on 3.66 acres. The massive 10,363-square-foot mansion includes the ten-bedroom main residence, a separate guest house and manicured grounds. The buyer also gets a zero-edge pool and spa, gardens, expansive terraces, and views from there that are simply breathtaking.The primary suite occupies an entire wing. It is bright, with a four-poster bed, and comes with a freestanding French bateau tub. It also has enough closet space to house a serious wardrobe collection. Even the laundry room is designed with the utmost care, and it simply reads as luxe, with two washers, two dryers and a folding island that would make Marie Kondo pause!The common spaces are the greatest attraction. They combine old-world French character with a very practical, lived-in layout. The home is designed for entertaining and gatherings, so the dining table can accommodate ten guests. The kitchen flows into a family living area with its own fireplace. The kitchen here is perfect for a chef and home cooks alike. It has professional-grade appliances sitting alongside antique finds.Just like other parts of the manor, it is a blend of modern looks and vintage charm. A massive island anchors the room, while built-in hutches display the china that’s already there, waiting. Behind an aged wooden door, there is a pantry holding everything a home chef could want for entertaining! The designer has already thought through the serving utensils, the glassware and the storage solutions.There’s a separate guest house on the grounds, stone-built and appointed with its own kitchen and bedroom, perfect for guests. And yet no one has lived here. Not once.A mansion designed to feel lived-in, filled with carefully curated pieces, is waiting for an owner who will presumably immediately make it their own by living in it. The asking price is $29 million. And that, too, is for a house no one has lived in yet. Plus, the manor comes with everything in it. The home arrives with antiques, gallery-acquired art and custom-made furniture included. Even the china in the hutches stays. The glassware lining the pantry shelves stays. The place settings tucked into the credenza drawers? Also staying.The listing calls the estate ‘un coin de paradis’, which translates to “a corner of paradise”. Maison de Campagne is basically a corner of paradise nestled in the Rancho Santa Fe Convent, a prestigious 6,000-acre residential community known for its ‘country-club lifestyle’, equestrian trails, dining, shopping and leisure at The Village. The buyer only has to walk in with their wardrobe!Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Trump takes trade war with Canada to ice
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: US-Canada ties hit the ice on Tuesday after MAGA boss Donald Trump threatened to shut Canadian aircraft maker B.
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: US-Canada ties hit the ice on Tuesday after MAGA boss Donald Trump threatened to shut Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier out of the American market unless it moves production to the US and Ottawa began imposing retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on about $20 billion of U.S. goods after Washington imposed comparable tariffs on Canadian products.The sharp escalation in a trade war between two countries that once prided themselves on having the world's least dramatic border was accompanied by bizarre theatrics from Washington, where Trump supporters reveled in memes showing the US President beating up Canadian PM Mark Carney in a hockey rink.The violent meme, an animated version of the Trump post showing him towering over Carney with the caption “GET UP, GOVERNOR” -- a jab tied to his insistence that Canada would be better off as America’s 51st state -- outraged many commentators on both sides of the border. “This video is disgusting, an embarrassment to all Americans. To me at least, it suggests mental instability on the part of Trump and underscores the patience and firm, measured dignity with which Prime Minister Carney has managed an out-of-control bully,” noted NYT columnist Nicholas Kristoff.Many Canadians mocked the video, reminding MAGAts chortling over the confrontation that Carney, 61, was an accomplished hockey player who was a goalie at Harvard and played for Edmonton Oilers, and should Trump, 80, take to the rink, he’d be on his backside in no time.But in Washington, where trade policy is normally conducted with briefing papers and acronyms, the North American relationship has lately acquired the atmosphere of a rowdy sports bar. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rubbed it into Ottawa over the weekend by comparing Canada to a “yippy little dog” like a dachshund snapping at the heels of a German Shepherd (USA) as the long celebrated ties between neighbors and close allies went to the dogs.On Monday, Trump dropped another bombshell by singling out the Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier. "NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren't good enough!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, arguing that more than 50 percent of Bombardier's revenue comes from the US, while Canada blocks companies such as Gulfstream Aerospace from doing business there. In yet another show of cartographic trolling, Trump also shared a post showing all of Canada and Mexico, as also Central America, the Caribbean, Greenland. and Iceland, in American flag colors. Iceland called in the U.S ambassador on Monday to protest.Ironically, Bombardier underscores the deeply intertwined economic ties between the two countries. It employs more than 3,000 people in the US and works with roughly 2,800 American companies across 47 states, and because of its substantial American footprint, is seen as a prime example of the difficulty Trump will have with his peculiar fixation of punishing Canada.The US, with its vastly larger economy clearly has the bigger stick according to trade experts. Carney acknowledged as much in a video post on Tuesday, saying while he didn’t believe in escalating the conflict, the harsh reality is that the American tariffs will hurt some Canadians. “This won’t be easy, and I won’t pretend otherwise,” he said, pledging to protect Canadians affected by the US trade war.But Canada, which sends roughly 68% of its exports south of the border, is hardly standing on an empty rink. It supplies the U.S with crucial energy, electricity and raw materials, while Canadian purchases support factories and farms across numerous American states. Carney has pointed out that Canada is the biggest customer for US goods in 26 states while urging Washington to stop “doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough” and start negotiating seriously.Instead, Washington has doubled down on the memes, while seriously expecting Ottawa to fold.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder case: Lawyer asks Trump to pardon Massachusetts mother after mistrial
articles.summary: US News: Attorney Kevin Reddington appeals to President Trump for a pardon for Lindsay Clancy, whose trial ended in mistrial after she was accused of killing her three children amidst claims of postpartum psychosis.
articles.body: The lawyer representing Lindsay Clancy, whose trial over the deaths of her three children ended without a verdict, has asked President Donald Trump to pardon her despite the case being prosecuted under Massachusetts state law.Attorney Kevin Reddington made the appeal during an interview with ABC's Good Morning America on Tuesday, urging Trump to consider Clancy's circumstances and her mental state."Mr. President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady, the type of person she is and what she’s been through, and consider a pardon," Reddington said.Clancy, 36, was accused of killing her three children at their home in January 2023. Her defence argued that she was not criminally responsible because she had suffered postpartum psychosis and was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time of the killings.Prosecutors disputed that account and argued that the killings were premeditated.The case ended in a mistrial last week after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. The state could still pursue a retrial.Trump had previously commented on the case after the mistrial was declared, saying Clancy had done "a horrible, horrible thing" but suggesting that her eventual punishment could involve imprisonment or treatment in a mental institution.The president's constitutional pardon authority generally covers federal offences, while Clancy's prosecution was brought under Massachusetts law. Trump's office was asked about Reddington's request on Tuesday and referred to the president's earlier remarks.Trump has previously used clemency in a case prosecuted under state law. In December, he pardoned former Colorado county clerk Tina Peters, a political ally who had been convicted of state charges linked to voting machine tampering, according to Reuters.The pardon did not directly release Peters from her state sentence, but it increased pressure on Colorado Governor Jared Polis, who later granted her clemency in May. Peters subsequently appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Paul Givan: Children with a parent on benefits will not be eligible for priority pre-school place
articles.summary: The Education Authority said "arrangements to implement the change will begin immediately".
articles.body:
Most children with a parent on benefits will not be eligible for priority nursery places from next year under changes to the rules announced by Education Minister Paul Givan.

The minister said he believed the rules - known as Socially Disadvantaged Circumstances (SDC) criterion - were not "lawful" and were "discriminating against hard-working families".

He added that the move would "level the playing field" for pre-school admissions.

However, critics have said the rules made sure vulnerable children got "a foot up the ladder", while political representatives from Sinn Féin, Alliance and the SDLP questioned the plans at Stormont on Monday.

The Education Authority (EA) said "arrangements to implement the change will begin immediately".

Givan announced his department was to repeal the SDC criterion and was launching a consultation to gather views on whether new legislation was also needed.

What has Paul Givan announced around pre-school places?

The SDC criterion, first introduced in 1998, provides the basis for underprivileged families to get priority pre-school placements.

The criterion allows the children of parents in receipt of benefits - specifically Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, Employment and Support Allowance and Universal Credit - to get priority for a pre-school place.

Income Support and Jobseeker's Allowance, however, no longer exist and have been replaced by Universal Credit.

Speaking in the assembly on Monday, Givan said the context of pre-school places is "very different" compared to when the SDC criterion were introduced.

He said welfare reforms meant that the officials had "read in" new welfare payments, such as Universal Credit, a payment he described as "significantly wider" than those named in the SDC legislation.

He added: "The current practice is also no longer legally defensible."

Givan said that only benefits specifically named in the legislation - Income Support and Jobseeker's Allowance - would be applied as SDC criteria from September 2027.

He added that as those benefits "have been phased out or superseded" he expected a "negligible number of applications" under SDC criterion next year.

He told BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show on Tuesday morning that limiting the number of benefit claims that qualify a child for a priority placement will "level the playing field in preschool admissions for hard working families".

"They're not middle-class. They're working-class people who are struggling, and their children have been disadvantaged," he said.

Some assembly members criticised the move when unveiled by Givan in the Stormont chamber on Monday, with one - Sinn Féin's Danny Baker - at one point describing him as "a disgrace".

In questioning the move, SDLP's Cara Hunter asked why he was removing the only statutory protection for children living "in absolute poverty", while Alliance's Nick Mathison said it was "something that could further disadvantage the children who are at the highest risk of educational disadvantage".

In response, Givan said it was about not taking a blanket approach, adding that "those struggling to make end meets" should not be disadvantaged because they work.

Dr Ciara Fitzpatrick, a lecturer at Ulster University, said SDC had been used to create an early education selection system that gave "our most vulnerable children" a "foot up on the ladder".

Fitzpatrick said research showed children from working class backgrounds tended to be "educationally further ahead" than their peers from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, and argued the education minister's plans would widen this disparity.

"Pre-school education is not about childcare, it's about early education.

"The evidence suggests that those children from socially deprived backgrounds have less communication skills, less school-readiness, less social skills.

"It means that early education is so important for them.

"It's going to stick by them as they go through school."

She also questioned how the move would affect how many hours a child would get a pre-school.

Currently, there is no standardised set hours for pre-school children across Northern Ireland, with some getting 12.5 hours of pre-school and others getting 22.5.

"Those less affluent children are prioritised for 22.5 hours because that is going to ensure they are not on the backfoot as they enter into primary school."

On Monday, the education minister said those getting 22.5 hours of pre-school had grown significantly during his time, from 40% of pupils two years ago to 65% now.

He added that the executive has committed to delivering standardised full-time pre-school hours but that the Department of Finance need to make the money available to do so.

Meanwhile, speaking to The Nolan Show, Fitzpatrick said she understood "working-class parents have frustrations but that's not on the back of these three and four-year-old children."

She said it is a "crude measure that is going to impact our most vulnerable children".

At a mother-and-toddler group in north Belfast, some parents welcomed the move saying it would be positive for working parents.

Carolyn, who has a six-year-old and three-year-old, told BBC News NI she works full-time and spends up to £600 a month on childcare.

"I do think it's a bit more positive because you feel like you're kind of being penalised for working," she said, while at the group at Woodvale Community Centre.

"If I didn't work then my child would have got that place and they're able to go out and thrive in an educational environment with less time between my house and the nanny's.

"I do feel it's a real positive that everyone's going to be on equal footing because as much as it's not classed as a childcare going to a preschool place, it still helps the working parents."

Ashton, who has two-year-old twin daughters, said she worked two days a week and is on benefits. However, she was unsuccessful in an application to get her daughters a two-year place.

"I still think that it should just be equal, for people that are on benefits and people that are in work, they shouldn't be treated any differently."

articles.title: Former Delhi chief secretary Rakesh Mehta found hanging at Noida residence, dies by suicide
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former Delhi chief secretary Rakesh Mehta, who served during chief minister Sheila Dikshit’s tenure, allegedly died by suicide at his resid.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Delhi chief secretary Rakesh Mehta, who served during chief minister Sheila Dikshit’s tenure, allegedly died by suicide at his residence in Noida, officials said on Tuesday.Mehta, 74, a 1975-batch IAS officer, was found hanging from a ceiling fan at his Sector 82 residence on September 6, officials told news agency PTI.Noida Police recovered a purported suicide note in which he cited his "mental and health issues" as the reasons behind the extreme step.Mehta's body was cremated at the Lodhi Road crematorium on Monday.Mehta served as Delhi's chief secretary for more than three years, taking charge in 2007 and retiring in November 2010. The 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi were organised during his tenure.He was credited with overseeing the execution of several key transport, power and civic infrastructure projects in the national capital.Mehta held several positions in the Delhi government during his career and also served as commissioner of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, according to his former colleagues.(with inputs from PTI)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Earthquake of magnitude 5.0 hits flood-ravaged Nepal
articles.summary: Rest of World News: NEW DELHI: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Nepal at 9.38 pm on Tuesday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, as the region continues t.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Nepal at 9.38 pm on Tuesday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, as the region continues to grapple with the aftermath of devastating flash floods that have killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal.The tremor was reported hours after a magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC). The Tibet quake occurred at a depth of 35 km.The latest tremors come days after another earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Tibet on Thursday last week, according to data from the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ). That earthquake was recorded at a depth of 10 km.The earthquakes come as the Tibet-Nepal region continues to reel from devastating flash floods that struck on August 26.The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River. The disaster devastated settlements across northern and central Nepal and damaged several hydropower projects.Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the death toll from the floods had risen to 1,357 as of Tuesday, with rescue teams continuing searches for 5,326 people. A total of 13,583 people had been rescued.Security forces recovered hundreds of bodies from affected districts including Chitawan, Nawalparasi East and West, Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahu. Authorities said 102 bodies had been handed over to families after identification and completion of legal formalities.At least 43 people were also killed on the Chinese side, while more than 500 remained missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.The floods washed away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaged hydropower infrastructure. Rescue operations were also underway at hydropower projects where 121 people were believed to be trapped in underground tunnels.The disaster has also raised concerns over the fragile environment of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, with Chinese climate experts pointing to rising temperatures, accelerated glacier melt, local geological and geomorphological conditions and broader climatic influences as possible contributing factors.Sun Xiaoguang, head of the Meteorological Observatory of the Tibet Autonomous Region, said: “According to our monitoring, we can see the short-time rain days, or the imbalance of the rain pattern and the rising of the temperature in Tibet.”He said the region could be affected by the climate change crisis and that extreme weather events in China could become more frequent.Chinese officials said Tibet has about 33,000 glaciers, including 187 classified as high-risk and requiring round-the-clock satellite monitoring to predict possible collapses, according to PTI.Kang Shichang, director and researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said glaciers across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau had shrunk by about 24% in area over the past six decades.In the southern part of the plateau, including the Himalayas, glacier coverage had fallen by about 40% over the same period, Kang told Chinese daily The Paper, attributing the retreat primarily to global warming.The scale of the disaster has also renewed scrutiny of hydropower projects in Tibet, including China's planned mega dam on the Brahmaputra River.The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau is the source of around 10 transboundary rivers, including the Brahmaputra, making changes to its glaciers, rivers and extreme weather patterns significant for downstream regions.Chinese researchers have linked the growing risks in the region to glacier retreat and climate change as authorities continue rescue and recovery operations following the August 26 floods.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: She bought a Maine island to stop clear-cutting; 90 years after Audubon opened its first camp there, the 330-acre sanctuary still trains conservationists
articles.summary: US News: Deep in Maine's Muscongus Bay, a 330-acre island covered in spruce trees has survived a threat of clear-cut logging and, 90 years later, continues to .
articles.body: Deep in Maine's Muscongus Bay, a 330-acre island covered in spruce trees has survived a threat of clear-cut logging and, 90 years later, continues to serve as an international training centre for environmentalists and bird researchers. Hog Island Audubon Camp, near the coastal community of Bremen, marked its 90th anniversary in late August 2026. According to records from the National Audubon Society and the Seabird Institute, the island was saved from commercial logging in the 1930s by Millicent Todd Bingham and her mother, Mabel Loomis Todd. Today, the island is the National Audubon Society's flagship educational camp, welcoming hundreds of scientists, teachers, artists and nature lovers every summer.From timber threat to national sanctuaryThe island's modern conservation story began during the Great Depression. Landowners had planned to clear-cut Hog Island's thick spruce forest, which included centuries-old wolf trees, large trees that had been left behind by earlier farmers to provide shade for livestock. Mabel Loomis Todd, a writer and editor best known for publishing the poetry of Emily Dickinson, recognised the value of the untouched forest and tried to buy the property. After her death in 1932, her daughter, Millicent Todd Bingham, a geographer and scholar, continued the effort. Bingham spent years working to secure the island and create a permanent plan to protect it. In 1936, she joined forces with John H. Baker, then executive director of the National Association of Audubon Societies, now known as the National Audubon Society. Together, they established Audubon's first Nature Study Camp. The programme was created to train primary and secondary school teachers in outdoor field biology. The teachers could then take what they learned back to classrooms across the United States. Historical records from the Todd Wildlife Sanctuary show that Bingham eventually gave the island to the National Audubon Society. This created a permanent refuge for wildlife and migratory seabirds.A landmark anniversary in Muscongus BayFrom 20 to 23 August 2026, more than 200 former campers, instructors, researchers and volunteers gathered on Hog Island to mark 90 years of continuous operation. According to an anniversary report from the National Audubon Society's Seabird Institute, the celebration included panel discussions, guided walks to study plants and tours of historic buildings, including the rustic Bingham cottages and the old Fish House. During a panel called "The Future is Bright at Hog Island," Audubon Chief Conservation Officer Marshall Johnson, along with instructors Maggie Dewane and Anthony Hill, discussed plans to expand research on the island over the next decade while keeping environmental education at its centre. The anniversary also recognised the Friends of Hog Island (FOHI), a volunteer group that helps keep the camp running. Its volunteers provide thousands of hours of work each summer, helping with building maintenance, kitchen duties, habitat management and fundraising for the Hog Island Endowment.Scientific innovation and artistic residencyHog Island has also played an important role in modern seabird conservation. In the 1970s, ornithologist Stephen Kress launched Project Puffin from the island. He developed social attraction methods, including wooden puffin decoys and recorded bird calls, to bring Atlantic Puffins back to nearby Eastern Egg Rock. The methods developed through the project at Hog Island are now used around the world to help restore threatened seabird colonies. The island also has a strong connection to the arts. According to National Audubon Society programme guidelines, the Hog Island Artist-in-Residence programme welcomes writers, visual artists and musicians each year. They stay in the historic Bingham cottages, continuing the creative tradition linked to Mabel Loomis Todd. Ninety years after its founding, the 330-acre island remains a living laboratory for conservation. As climate change and rising sea levels reshape New England's coastal waters, the research and education carried out at Hog Island continue to influence bird conservation efforts across North America.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A ship that sank in the Baltic Sea in the 1850s may have been carrying luxury gifts for a Russian king, including champagne bottles and mineral water
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A 19th-century shipwreck lying beneath the Baltic Sea may have been carrying a lavish cargo intended for the Russian imperial court, including more th.
articles.body: A 19th-century shipwreck lying beneath the Baltic Sea may have been carrying a lavish cargo intended for the Russian imperial court, including more than 100 bottles of champagne, wine, mineral water and porcelain. Divers from the Polish group Baltictech discovered the wreck off Sweden’s Öland island after initially mistaking it for a fishing boat. The clay bottles of Selters mineral water helped date the vessel to between 1850 and 1867, while the nature of the cargo has raised the possibility that it was bound for Tsar Nicholas I. Baltictech leader Tomasz Stachura said the mineral water was once an exclusive product associated with royal tables and suggested the ship may have been travelling towards Stockholm or St Petersburg. The theory remains unconfirmed, but it gains historical context from research into other Baltic shipwreck champagne, which found that Russian customers preferred particularly sweet wines.Luxury cargo points to a Russian kingOne of the clues behind the theory is the presence of Selters mineral-water bottles. The clay bottles carried the name of the German company Selters and helped researchers date the wreck to between 1850 and 1867. As reported by the BBC, mineral water was not an ordinary drink at the time but an expensive product “treated almost like medicine” that reached royal tables. He also said its value was so high that some transports were escorted by police.The combination of mineral water, champagne, wine and porcelain therefore makes the wreck different from the cheaper commercial cargoes divers commonly encounter. Stachura said: “Usually, when we find wrecks, the cargo is very cheap.” He believes the ship may have been travelling across the Baltic towards Stockholm or St Petersburg; a route would fit the possibility of an imperial destination, although there is currently no definitive evidence of the intended recipient.Why did Russian customers prefer sweeter champagneHistorical research into champagne recovered from another Baltic Sea shipwreck shows just how important the Russian market was to champagne producers during the 19th century. According to the study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, titled ‘Chemical messages in 170-year-old champagne bottles from the Baltic Sea: Revealing tastes from the past’, 170-year-old bottles were recovered from a wreck near Finland’s Åland archipelago. Researchers found 168 bottles, with cork markings identifying champagne from Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin, Heidsieck and Juglar.The study found that Russian customers had developed a particularly strong preference for sweet champagne. According to historical correspondence, Russian customers could request a sugar dosage approaching 300 grams per litre. They always have some sugar on any table close to their wine glass. However, the researchers noted that the Baltic wreck bottles contained less than 150 grams of sugar per litre, meaning that particular shipment may instead have been intended for customers in the Germanic Confederation.How underwater wrecks kept champagne well preservedThe earlier Baltic champagne discovery also demonstrates why bottles that spent more than a century underwater can remain remarkably well preserved. The bottles were found at about 50 metres below the surface, where darkness, temperatures of roughly 2–4°C, low salinity and high pressure created what researchers described as nearly ideal conditions for slow ageing. The PNAS study said the champagne samples provided an unprecedented opportunity to examine how wine changed over 170 years.The more recently discovered wreck lies even deeper, at around 58 metres. Wine writer Henry Jeffreys told the BBC that the cold and darkness provide long-term storage, saying: “If you're going to leave champagne for 150 plus years, the bottom of the sea is a really good place.” He cautioned that the champagne may have lost most of its fizz, but depending on the condition of the corks, it could still be “palatable”.Researchers continue to investigate the wreckFor now, the idea that the cargo was destined for Tsar Nicholas I remains a theory rather than a confirmed historical fact. The available evidence the wreck’s date, its location, the prestigious mineral water and the unusually luxurious cargo provides intriguing clues, but researchers still need archival evidence to establish where the vessel was travelling and who was meant to receive its goods. Stachura himself acknowledged that the historical investigation could take longer than the diving itself, saying: “But then diving into the archives is what can be more interesting.”The cargo also was not immediately brought to the surface. Underwater archaeologists have been called in, Swedish authorities have been notified, and administrative procedures must be completed before any recovery can take place. Stachura believes there is no need to rush, noting that the wreck has already remained underwater for around 170 years. As he put it: “It had been lying there for 170 years, so let it lie there one more year.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Erika Kirk pens essay on grief as readers gain insights into wrenching past year
articles.summary: Erika Kirk penned a New York Times essay on grief as the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk's fatal shooting at Utah Valley University approaches.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — A year after Erika Kirk endured the unimaginable tragedy of her husband Charlie's assassination, she shared what she's learned about the universality of grief in a New York Times guest essay. Kirk, who took over leadership of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) following the fatal shooting of her 31-year-old husband Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, penned the piece Monday that's headlined, "What I’ve learned about grief." She feels Americans increasingly experience each other through political labels and wanted to write something that reminds everyone that grief is something everyone can share. ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY "You do not have to share someone’s politics, faith or worldview to understand what it means to lose someone you love. She wanted to meet people on common human ground and speak honestly about what the past year has been like," a TPUSA source told Fox News Digital. Much of what she has been through over the past year is deeply familiar to anyone who has grieved, and she detailed how hard it was to make it through the first holidays and family milestones without her husband. Erika Kirk explained why simply getting "through the next 15 minutes," which was advice from second lady Usha Vance, has been critical in getting through the past year. JD VANCE'S WIFE USHA DETAILS HOW CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH INFLUENCED DECISION TO HAVE FOURTH CHILD "The first Saturday without a love note from him passed. His 32nd birthday. My birthday. Thanksgiving. When I put the Christmas tree together wrong, it made me realize that being a widow means old traditions will need to make room for new ones. The wave crashes on me again and again. Every time, just get through the next 15 minutes," Kirk wrote in the Times. "Grief is strange. Time continues even when every part of you wants it to pause or, better yet, rewind. But the people we love who have passed on would not want us to spend the rest of our lives trying to rewind," she continued. "At first, I needed to survive the next 15 minutes. Over time, I’ve realized that Charlie would want me to live them." Over the past 12 months, Kirk has tried to carry her late husband’s mission forward. She does not believe the answer to his death is to retreat further into separate camps where people only speak to those who already agree with them. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION "He deliberately went into places where there was disagreement and invited people who saw the world differently to talk to him. He said, ‘When people stop talking, really bad stuff starts,’" the TPUSA source said. Charlie Kirk founded TPUSA to promote conservatism on college campuses nationwide. He was speaking before more than 2,000 people at a TPUSA event in Orem, Utah, when he was assassinated, leaving behind Erika and their two children. articles.title: In 1973, Montana released a gall fly to control spotted knapweed; decades later, the biocontrol program was linked to over 3 times more hantavirus-positive deer mice
articles.summary: US News: A biological control project started half a century ago to destroy a stubborn invasive weed accidentally set off an ecological chain reaction that inc.
articles.body: A biological control project started half a century ago to destroy a stubborn invasive weed accidentally set off an ecological chain reaction that increased human exposure to a deadly virus. In 1973, wildlife officials and agricultural scientists in Montana released two species of European gall flies, Urophora affinis and Urophora quadrifasciata, to control the spread of spotted knapweed (Centaurea stoebe). Decades later, major research published in Ecology Letters and archived by the US Forest Service Treesearch database found that the flies became a common winter food source for native deer mice (Peromyscus maniculatus). The extra food helped mouse populations grow and increased the spread of Sin Nombre hantavirus. As a result, knapweed-infested areas had more than three times as many hantavirus-positive deer mice as areas of native grassland without knapweed.A well-intentioned biocontrol interventionSpotted knapweed, an aggressive Eurasian perennial plant introduced to North America in the late 19th century, had spread across millions of acres of western rangeland by the middle of the 20th century. The weed takes over pastures, competes with native grasses, increases soil erosion and greatly reduces the amount of land available for livestock grazing. To control the weed without relying heavily on costly chemical herbicides, agricultural managers turned to classical biological control. According to an early study published in Environmental Entomology by Jim Story and Robert Nowak of the Montana Agricultural Experiment Station, Urophora affinis was introduced into Montana in 1973. Field trials had shown that the fly's larvae create galls inside knapweed seed heads, using the plant's nutrients and reducing the number of viable seeds produced. A second species, Urophora quadrifasciata, soon spread across the region. Entomologists initially considered the flies a success because large numbers of knapweed seed heads were being attacked in Western Montana.An unintended winter food sourceAlthough the gall flies became very common, they did not eliminate or greatly reduce the overall amount of spotted knapweed across the Northern Rockies. Instead, the large number of larvae created a rich and reliable winter food source for local wildlife. Research led by ecologist Dean E. Pearson of the US Department of Agriculture Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station, together with researchers from the University of Montana, showed how deer mice changed their winter feeding habits to take advantage of the introduced insects. During the cold autumn and winter months, when native seeds and insects are harder to find, deer mice spend more time feeding in knapweed patches. The mice open the dry seed heads and eat the gall fly larvae that remain inside through winter. Pearson's research team found that the larvae could make up as much as 85 per cent of a deer mouse's winter diet in heavily infested areas. This effectively removed the seasonal shortage of food that had previously helped keep mouse numbers under control.Rising rodent numbers and hantavirus riskThe extra winter food changed the local mouse population. With a steady food supply, deer mice in areas dominated by knapweed survived the winter at much higher rates. They also entered the spring breeding season in better physical condition than mice living in areas of native bunchgrass prairie. The increase in mice also created a public health concern. Deer mice are the main natural hosts of Sin Nombre virus, a hantavirus that can spread to people when they breathe in tiny particles from the urine, droppings or saliva of infected rodents. In humans, the virus can cause Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), a serious respiratory disease with a mortality rate of about 36 per cent, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In field studies examining this chain of effects, Pearson and his colleagues found that deer mouse numbers were twice as high in knapweed-infested areas. More importantly, the higher mouse density and increased contact between mice during aggressive winter feeding led to more virus transmission. Blood tests showed that knapweed sites had more than three times as many hantavirus-infected deer mice per hectare as native grassland sites.Implications for future invasive species managementThe connection between Urophora gall flies, spotted knapweed and hantavirus transmission is a well-known example of the unexpected effects that can follow biological control programmes. Instead of controlling the target weed, the introduced flies unintentionally provided extra food for a native disease-carrying animal. Later management guidance from the US Forest Service and state agriculture departments stressed the importance of studying possible effects across entire food webs before releasing non-native biological control agents. Modern approaches require scientists to consider not only whether an agent will attack its target weed, but also how it could affect local food chains and predator-prey relationships over many years. Across Montana, weed control efforts have increasingly moved towards combining several methods. These include reseeding native plants, planting competitive species and using host-specific root weevils such as Cyphocleonus achates to reduce knapweed without creating large populations of larvae that can become food for rodents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sapporo to move some production to US after 50% tariff
articles.summary: The Japanese brewer plans to shift non-alcoholic beer brewing to the US from Canada as tariffs bite
articles.body:
Japanese brewer Sapporo says it will move some beer production from Canada to the US after new tariffs on Canadian beer took effect on Tuesday .

The move follows the introduction of a 50% tariff on beer imported from Canada. For companies shipping beer across the border , that means significantly higher costs .

Chief strategy officer Rieko Shofu described tariffs as "something out of our control," telling Bloomberg that the beer giant would "move ahead with local production."

Sapporo did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment. The company plans to shift production of its non-alcoholic beer, currently made in Canada for US customers, to the US by the first half of 2027.

The US is one of Sapporo's most important overseas markets, and any shift south of the border will directly affect operations at its Canadian subsidiary, Sleeman Breweries.

To mitigate rising costs, the Japanese brewer is considering adding production capacity on the US West Coast. Options include building or buying a brewery, or partnering with a third-party manufacturer.

Sapporo has been building its presence in the US for years and says its flagship Sapporo brand is the country's best-selling Asian beer brand.

The company is also investing heavily outside Japan where a shrinking population has weighed on alcohol sales.

Sapporo plans to invest up to ¥400bn ($2.6bn) by 2030 as it seeks to expand overseas and boost profits. Around 30% of the capital is earmarked for overseas markets.

The brewer is also looking beyond North America. In July, it announced a partnership with Danish brewer Carlsberg to expand in Southeast Asia.

Sapporo's decision to move production comes as companies adapt to a growing number of tariffs worldwide.

In July, the US announced new tariffs on dozens of trading partners, including Canada, raising costs for businesses that rely on cross-border supply chains.

The move highlights how some companies are reconsidering where they make goods as trade barriers increase the cost of serving customers from overseas.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE The jet overshot the runway by at least 1,300 feet beyond the paved surface and crashed into multiple vehicles, including a 2012 white Ford Econoline van with passengers inside, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said during a Monday press conference. articles.title: United flight attendant makes quick save, catching baby that was about to fall from 'exhausted' mom's lap
articles.summary: Monique Harris says she had no idea "being my normal natural self" would go viral after catching a baby on a United Airlines flight from Newark.
articles.body: A flight attendant aboard a United Airlines flight sprang into action when an exhausted mother dozed off and her baby began slipping from her lap — catching the child before offering to hold the baby so the weary mom could get some much-needed rest. Passenger John Frehse shared the touching encounter on Instagram, praising flight attendant Monique Harris for her quick response aboard United flight 3486 from Newark, New Jersey, to Grand Rapids, Michigan. "United should be very proud," Frehse wrote, adding that the new mother had fallen asleep when her baby was "about to fall out of her lap." PILOT MARRIES VEGAS-BOUND COUPLE MID-FLIGHT AS 178 PASSENGERS BECOME WEDDING GUESTS "Monique sprung into action and caught the child," he wrote. "She then told the mother to go back to sleep - she would give her a break." Frehse also shared a photo appearing to show Harris holding the baby aboard the aircraft. "All is not lost in the turbulent time," he wrote. Frehse tagged United CEO Scott Kirby in the post and said he has flown more than 2 million miles with the airline. "She is an A+ employee," he wrote. "Take note!!!" RETIRED POLICE CHIEF HELPS SUBDUE PASSENGER AFTER ALLEGED MIDAIR OUTBURST OVER ALCOHOL CUTOFF Harris responded to the praise in the comments, saying she was moved by the attention the moment had received. "I’m in tears," she wrote, adding, "I never do anything for recognition." Harris said she "had no idea that being my normal natural self would grow into such a priceless moment," and thanked Frehse and others for the comments. Republic Airways, which operates flights for United and other airlines, praised Harris in an email to Fox News Digital. "We agree with all the positive comments I saw on the post: Monique is an extraordinary colleague and flight attendant!" the carrier said. The carrier also responded to the initial social media post, saying it was proud to have Harris on its team. "Such a great story!" the airline wrote. "We are proud to have Monique on our team." articles.title: Philippines defense chief calls out China after note interrupts remarks at Seoul forum: 'Coercion, bullying'
articles.summary: Gilberto Teodoro read aloud a note from China handed to him mid-speech at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, calling it actual coercion and bullying.
articles.body: Gilberto C. Teodoro, the Defense Secretary for the Philippines, publicly bashed China after he was handed a note outlining China's position on the South China Sea while he was speaking during the Seoul Defense Dialogue in South Korea on Tuesday. While Teodoro was in the middle of speaking, a man in a white sports coat walked up behind him and placed a sheet of paper on the table beside him. "I have a note here, I think this is from China," Teodoro said, stopping short in his remarks. "And may I read it?" he asked the crowd, before proceeding to read aloud from the note. "China's position on the South China Sea arbitration is clear, consistent and firm. They have no position. The arbitration violates fundamental principles of international law," the note read. MASSIVE RISK IN SOUTH CHINA SEA EXPOSED AFTER FOUR-DAY POWER LOSS ON US NAVY DESTROYER The note likely referred to the 2016 legal case that the Philippines brought against China under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The case, titled the South China Sea Arbitration, determined that China was unlawfully reclaiming land in the Philippines' territorial waters. China has long rebuked the ruling and consistently accuses the Philippines of infringing on China's sovereignty in the disputed waters. The long-running dispute has created a number of tense standoffs between the two countries' navies. "How can you deal with a country in an international forum – beyond the question asked to me – disrespecting the organizers of this forum, how do you expect to deal with it civilly?" Teodoro asked the crowd. "I ask you the question, is this the right paper to post to me when I'm being asked a question on the floor? And how will you treat this kind of behavior? It not only disrespects, shows, if this is a Chinese position sent to me, it not only disrespects international law, throwing UNCLOS to the floor and trampling upon it, but it also disrespects the basic decency accorded that should be accorded to our most gracious host, the Republic of Korea and the rest of the audience here," he continued. RULE JAPANICA: AMERICA AND JAPAN ARE BUILDING THE ALLIANCE CHINA FEARS "So, perhaps basic decency and behavior is what China needs to do. This is actual coercion, bullying and aggression. I will keep this paper as a memento of how desperate China is and how ineffective its position is in the face of a free audience. Thank you very much for the person who gave me this piece of paper. You have just done your country a great service," Teodoro added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think it is well known to the public, to everyone here about the Philippine situation where we face challenges daily from the People's Republic of China which tries to occupy and illegally assert its presence over our territory and especially our exclusive economic zone. In contravention with the UNCLOS. We live in a very interconnected world, and there is no right for any state of that matter to appropriate an international common for its exclusive use or right, contrary to what the international norms clearly state. So the Philippines has been forced to enter into creative defense arrangements and alliances," Teodoro concluded.

articles.title: Jack London bought 1,400 acres of exhausted California farmland and planted 65,000 eucalyptus trees; his experimental Beauty Ranch is now a state park
articles.summary: US News: The California ranch where Jack London spent his final years was not simply a country retreat for a wealthy author but a testing ground. London bought.
articles.body: The California ranch where Jack London spent his final years was not simply a country retreat for a wealthy author but a testing ground. London bought the Hill Ranch on Sonoma Mountain in 1905 and soon found that the land had been worn down by intensive farming. The discovery pushed him towards agriculture, a subject he pursued with unusual seriousness. He studied farming manuals, explored scientific approaches to soil management and began putting ideas into practice across the property. As he purchased neighbouring parcels, the ranch grew to roughly 1,400 acres and took the name Beauty Ranch. London planted enormous numbers of trees, raised cattle, horses and pigs, experimented with crops and built systems designed to recycle materials produced on the farm.He even tested spineless cactus as cattle feed with Luther Burbank, the world’s leading horticulturist. Some schemes failed or produced unexpected results, but the aim remained the same: restore the land while making the ranch increasingly self-sufficient. Much of that story remains preserved today.Jack London’s first California ranch revealed badly depleted farmlandJack London arrived at Sonoma Mountain with money made from his writing and a clear intention to make the Valley of the Moon his permanent home. In June 1905, while living with Charmian at Wake Robin Lodge in Glen Ellen, he bought the 130-acre Hill Ranch for $7,000, as reported by Jack London Historic Park.He described the property as some of the most beautiful primitive land in California. Yet the impression changed when he began preparing part of it for hay. Clearing about 40 acres exposed a problem that would shape his approach to farming for years: the soil had been repeatedly cropped without enough being returned to it.The surrounding ranches had also struggled. London eventually acquired several adjoining properties from owners who had failed financially, turning what had been a collection of troubled farms into a single expanding estate.Jack London turned his ranch into a living agricultural experimentLondon approached the problem as he approached many other subjects in his life; by reading. Agricultural manuals and scientific works became part of his study, and farming gradually took up far more of his working day than might be expected of a novelist.He came to reject the idea that a farm should simply extract as much as possible from its fields. His own rule was to keep material on the property wherever possible. Crop residues, animal manure and plants grown specifically to improve the soil all had a role.Jack London quoted, "I am rebuilding worn-out hillside lands that were worked out and destroyed by our wasteful California pioneer farmers. I believe the soil is our one indestructible asset, and by green manures, nitrogen-gathering cover crops, animal manure, rotation of crops, proper tillage and draining, I am getting results which the Chinese have demonstrated for forty centuries."Green manure became particularly important. Cover crops could be grown and then worked back into the ground, adding organic matter and helping replenish nutrients. Crop rotation was used instead of repeatedly planting the same crop, while drainage and careful tillage were part of the effort to make better use of the land.London also experimented with terracing. He had encountered the practice while working as a war correspondent in Korea in 1904, and later applied the principle to his California property as a means of limiting the loss of soil from sloping ground.Beauty Ranch grew into a large-scale farming operation for LondonThe Hill Ranch did not remain a small farm. London continued buying neighbouring parcels, and by 1913 his holdings on Sonoma Mountain covered about 1,400 acres. The property became known as Beauty Ranch, and London sometimes referred to it as the Ranch of Good Intentions.There was plenty happening across those acres. Hay was grown, livestock were kept and thousands of trees were planted. London eventually put about 65,000 eucalyptus trees into the ground and continued looking for ways to make unproductive acreage useful again.By 1916, close to 50 people were employed on the ranch. Farming was no longer a side project for a successful author. It had become a substantial operation occupying much of his time and attention.London tested new ideas to make the ranch more self-sufficientLondon was interested in practical experiments, even when the results were mixed. He worked with horticulturist Luther Burbank on growing spineless cactus as a possible source of cattle feed. The plants could grow quickly under the right conditions, but irrigation was needed, and some of the cactus eventually developed spines again.A small patch of the experiment survives in the meadow at the historic park.The ranch also had its own system for dealing with feed and animal waste. London built what has been described as California's first concrete-block silo, using it to store silage made from shredded corn stalks. The silage went to the dairy cattle, while the pigs were fed corn.Italian stonemasons were brought in to construct a barn for the horses, as well as a manure pit where animal waste could be collected and turned into fertiliser. The intention was to make the farm less dependent on outside inputs and to return useful material to the soil.Fields that had been considered exhausted produced againSome of London's most striking results came from land that had previously been regarded as badly overworked. He reported record oat-hay yields from fields that had suffered under earlier farming practices.His approach was not based on a single technique. The farm combined rotations, cover crops, manure, composting, terracing, drainage and controlled use of grazing animals. In his view, restoring the soil was as important as producing a crop from it.That thinking can be seen in a line London wrote about the property: he wanted to leave the land better because he had lived and worked there. His methods were shaped partly by his reading of agricultural science and partly by practices he had encountered elsewhere, including the long-established farming traditions of China.Beauty Ranch after LondonLondon died in 1916, aged 40, but the agricultural landscape he had developed remained an important part of the property. His former ranch is now protected as Jack London State Historic Park, covering roughly the same 1,400 acres that had been assembled during his lifetime.The park contains buildings and landscapes associated with the Londons, including the remains of the ranch's agricultural operations. Visitors can still encounter parts of the working landscape that made Beauty Ranch more than a retreat for a famous writer.Its significance lies partly in that unusual combination. London came to Sonoma Mountain as a novelist with an interest in farming and ended up devoting enormous amounts of time to restoring worn soil, raising animals and testing ideas in the fields. The ranch became a long-running experiment in whether damaged farmland could be made productive again without simply repeating the practices that had exhausted it in the first place.More than a century later, the land is no longer a private working ranch. But the fields, buildings and surviving traces of London's experiments remain within the state park, preserving an unusual chapter of his life that took place far from the writing desk.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1989, a Canadian couple bought 187 acres on Ontario’s Wilson Island as a family sanctuary; 36 years later, they donated it so its forests, wetlands and wildlife would stay protected
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Canadian couple who spent 36 years protecting a 187-acre island property as a private family sanctuary have donated the land to conservation, ensuri.
articles.body: A Canadian couple who spent 36 years protecting a 187-acre island property as a private family sanctuary have donated the land to conservation, ensuring its forests, wetlands and wildlife remain protected for generations to come.Jim and Anne Purvis purchased the 187.4-acre property on Wilson Island in Ontario’s Trent Hills area in 1989. Over the following decades, they stewarded the land with the goal of preserving and restoring its ecological integrity.According to a media release, the property, which the couple named Inscape, has now been acquired by the Northumberland Land Trust (NLT). The conservation organisation announced the completed acquisition on January 7, 2026.Rather than developing or selling the land, the Purvis family chose to place it under long-term conservation protection.187 acres of forests, wetlands and natural habitatLocated at the western tip of Wilson Island, Inscape sits directly beside Murray Marsh, an area identified as an Area of Natural and Scientific Interest (ANSI).Almost 100 per cent of the property remains in a natural state, according to the Northumberland Land Trust.Around 130 acres consist of regionally significant woodlands, while much of the property is identified as a provincially significant wetland.The reserve contains several distinct ecosystems, including deciduous swamps, thicket swamps, cattail marshes, grassland and a vernal pool.The combination of habitats makes the property an important refuge for wildlife and contributes to the health of the surrounding ecosystem.Eight species at risk found on the propertyThe land is also home to several species considered at risk.Species identified on the property include the Least Bittern, Red-headed Woodpecker and Midland Painted Turtle, alongside other species such as the Eastern Meadowlark, Black Tern, Eastern Wood-pewee, Wood Thrush and Snapping Turtle.The property lies within the Trent River, but changes to water levels following the installation of dams have made the island land increasingly difficult to access.Because of its sensitive ecological features and difficult access, Inscape will remain closed to the public.The decision means the land will function primarily as a protected natural area rather than a public recreation site.Couple wanted the land protected ‘in perpetuity’The Purvis family had spent decades caring for the property before deciding to transfer its long-term stewardship to the land trust.“We have stewarded Inscape for 36 years for the purpose of protecting and restoring its ecological integrity,” Jim and Anne Purvis said.They added that they were excited to work with the Northumberland Land Trust's conservation expertise and network to preserve Inscape “as a natural area where plants, animals, birds will flourish in perpetuity.”The property was initially announced as a future land-trust acquisition in May 2025, when the NLT said it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Purvis family.At the time, Rob Kennedy, president of the Northumberland Land Trust, said the Purvises had purchased the property in 1989 and used it as a natural sanctuary for their family for the next 35 years.A family effort to preserve the landThe conservation project also became a family fundraising effort.Amanda Newell, executive director of the Northumberland Land Trust, said the Purvis property became a cornerstone of the organisation's 2025 fundraising campaign.The campaign helped offset administrative expenses associated with accepting the donation while also supporting the long-term stewardship of the property.The Purvis family's commitment extended beyond Jim and Anne. Their son, Michael Purvis, made a substantial contribution to the fundraising campaign, helping the organisation surpass its fundraising target.“Their commitment truly became a family affair,” Newell said.Why land donations are important for conservationDonating land to a conservation organisation is not simply a matter of handing over a property deed.According to the Northumberland Land Trust, conservation land donations can involve appraisals, severances, surveys, legal documentation and township approvals.The process can cost as much as $40,000, in addition to the ongoing expenses associated with managing and stewarding protected land.Fundraising and donations therefore play an important role in enabling conservation organisations to accept properties and maintain them over the long term.For Inscape, those efforts will allow the Northumberland Land Trust to continue the conservation work started by the Purvis family more than three decades ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Abuse of RNLI volunteers 'wholly unacceptable', chief says
articles.summary: Peter Sparkes says there has been "deliberate misinformation" spread about the charity.
articles.body:
RNLI staff have faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse since anti-migrant protests at the weekend, the charity's chief executive has said.

On Sunday, police faced off with demonstrators who blocked roads in Portsmouth in an effort to stop 140 people who arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area with the RNLI's assistance.

Chief executive Peter Sparkes said the abuse of volunteers was "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

He said there had been "deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding" about the charity, and condemned threats by "those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard".

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill .

Footage was subsequently posted on social media showing volunteers of the Poole-based charity labelled as "traitors".

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He continued: "We will take whatever steps we can, to care for and protect our people and their families."

Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy said she had spoken with tech firms about how the names, addresses and photographs of RNLI staff and volunteers were reportedly shared online.

She was responding to Vikki Slade, the Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Dorset and North Poole, about "some very disturbing posts" on social media identifying "brave RNLI rescuers".

Nandy was asked what more the government could do to remove posts "that put children and adults' safety at risk through doxxing".

She told the Commons: "It is something that the government is concerned about [and] I'm personally concerned about."

Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying the migrants were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port, the BBC understands .

Sparkes described illegal migration as a "polarising subject" and urged people to "be mindful of misinformation" and the "impact it has upon others".

He said: "Be reassured that the RNLI and our crews strive only to prevent people like you and me from drowning at sea.

"Stand by them, not against them and their families.

"I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work that meant 389 families welcomed their loved one homes safely last year."

Of the 9,058 RNLI lifeboat launches in 2025, 109 were to those "in distress in the Channel", Sparkes said, which makes up 1.2% of the charity's total rescue work.

He said nearly 95% of small boats were intercepted by the UK Border Force.

"Our mission, and our tasking is to rescue those women, children and men in danger of drowning," he added.

articles.title: Tim Montgomerie quits Reform following suspension
articles.summary: The political commentator, who defected from the Tories 18 months ago, was suspended from Reform UK last month.
articles.body:
Conservative Party defector and political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told the BBC he has resigned from Reform UK, urging Nigel Farage to "get a grip" of the party.

Montgomerie defected from the Tories 18 months ago but was suspended from Reform UK last month after he criticised senior figures.

His decision to resign came after a conversation with Reform's party chair Lee Anderson on Tuesday. "I think they wanted me back in the party but meekly," he told the BBC. "And I wasn't prepared to do that."

Montgomerie said he still plans to support Reform and has no intention of re-joining the Conservatives.

"I want to still be a supporter, but that requires them being more like Reform and less like the AfD [Germany's right-wing Alternative for Deutschland]", he said.

The far-right AfD won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhal this weekend, in what commentators said was a watershed moment as no far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants.

In the wake of controversial demonstrations against migrants in Dover and Portsmouth linked to Tommy Robinson this week, Montgomerie suggested Nigel Farage needs to go further in asserting his authority and professionalising the party.

"Nigel needs to get a grip, he needs to lead the party", he said.

"The one thing he's been brilliant at is policing the right and stopping [far-right activist] Tommy Robinson joining.

"But for the sake of his legacy and the sake of decency he needs to sort it out, and bring people like Zia [Yusuf] under control."

Last month, Montgomerie told the BBC he was frustrated at Farage's "aggrieved" tone after the Clacton by-election - and told the Spectator podcast that Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf was not a "team player".

At the time, Reform said he had been suspended "in line with party rules" after public criticism of the party.

Montgomerie joined Reform after a long career as a Tory adviser and commentator, and he had run the ConservativeHome website.

In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he still believed in Reform's policies and its membership, and he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms.

Following his decision to quit, Montgomerie said: "I'm feeling very sad about it, I feel battered by it... When you get older there's less fight in you.

"Reform is at a junction: They haven't replaced the Conservatives which was plan A. I fear a battle of attrition between the two parties which will helps no one. The real danger now on the fight for political turf is that they go after sectional interests.

"Does Reform want to be a party of government or does it want to stand at the edge and just change the debate?"

A Reform UK spokesman said: "We wish Tim the best for the future and thank him for his support."
